## Discussion

By reanalyzing reads that transcriptomic pipelines usually discard, we show that cutaneous HPV is active in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) and transcriptionally silent in healthy skin. In cSCC and actinic keratosis it appears only as a trace, which neither greater sequencing depth nor better library chemistry turns into productive infection. Prior RNA-seq and in situ reports of silence in cutaneous carcinoma [@arron2011; @hultin2019; @arroyomuhr2021; @vandiver2021; @fujimoto2019], and a recent review reporting beta-HPV as typically transcriptionally inactive in immunocompetent patients [@bruyere2026], gain from this work the controls, denominator and defined metric they lacked: `r comma(stats$neo_n)` cSCC/AK and `r comma(stats$uns_n)` unselected-skin libraries in one pipeline, where the same instrument that finds no productive infection in cSCC/AK reports `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% productivity in warts.

This result does not settle the mechanism, because all three models predict a declining viral signal along progression. Hit-and-run works because ultraviolet-induced host mutations can make E6 and E7 dispensable once a tumor is established [@viarisio2018], after which it may be lost from the expanding clone; protective immunity because virus-positive cells face negative selection [@strickley2019; @son2025]; cis-restriction because quiescence is the viral default [@rehm2022]. A fourth consideration is a property of the readout rather than a model: late transcription requires terminal differentiation [@doorbar2012], so a poorly differentiated tumor cannot run the late program regardless. Our trace decomposition answers both that requirement and the broader objection that an oncogene-driven mechanism needs E6/E7 function rather than capsid production, since `r tr("trace_pct_nogene")`% of below-floor skin and neoplasia libraries carry no reads on any HPV gene at all, not merely no late ones (@suppfig-trace). Distinguishing only transcription from its absence, our data cannot separate the three models. Nor does absent transcription imply clearance: episomal genomes may persist silently, or with intermittent activity, below the detection limit of bulk RNA sequencing, and absence in established lesions does not exclude a transient viral contribution earlier in carcinogenesis.

The elevated beta-HPV activity Son and colleagues found in keratinocyte clones of sun-exposed skin [@son2025] does not conflict with our silent reservoir: we sequenced whole biopsies without sorting for ultraviolet exposure, and a signal arising from small keratinocyte clones is diluted when averaged across an entire biopsy, a documented effect for cutaneous HPV [@purdie2005]. We nevertheless agree on viral presence, recovering trace HPV from `r pp(stats$ak_pctany)`% of AK libraries. HPV8 was absent at any level from all `r comma(rvn("n_rna_all"))` analyzed RNA libraries, which argues against persistent productive HPV8 transcription in established lesions while remaining compatible with transient, focal or latent activity. The nine-valent vaccine, which reduced actinic keratosis burden in a randomized trial [@wenande2025], targets mucosal alpha types rather than this beta reservoir.

The rare productive infections we do find in primary skin are beta-HPV, mucosal HPV16 excepted (@supptbl-cin), which constrains how the trace result should be read. Outside warts and EV, three primary-skin lesions carry unambiguous productive infection by a cutaneous type: an HPV12-productive cSCC, and two actinic-keratosis/cSCC libraries co-infected with HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage and high depth. These types belong to the beta-HPV species Betapapillomavirus 1, 5 and 2 respectively, so the genus running a complete productive program in these lesions is the same genus the cofactor debate concerns. Productive beta-HPV infection of primary skin is therefore possible but rare, and the silence we report in cutaneous neoplasia is not a ceiling on what beta-HPV can do in skin. No productive HPV12, HPV96 or HPV182 has to our knowledge been described from public RNA-seq of primary skin.

A 2–3% active transcription rate does not contradict a 90% viral DNA reservoir, for three reasons. Beta-HPV DNA loads sit below one copy per 60 cells [@weissenborn2012], beneath the detection limit of bulk RNA sequencing. The tissue sources differ: skin epidemiology studies test surface swabs and hair bulbs (92% and 73% prevalence) [@rollison2019sites], whereas RNA-seq uses deep biopsies that miss surface and hair follicle layers. And screening panels miss 229 skin types lacking reference genomes [@bzhalava2014]. The reservoir also differs from the viruses found in tumors: fewer than 5% of skin types match later cSCC [@rollison2021], and paired eyebrow hair and cSCC showed only 9.1% genotype concordance in another cohort [@oh2026].

Unadjusted analyses are dominated by contamination. Cultured materials show a five-fold enrichment reflecting known archival HeLa contamination [@cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015; @adey2013], traced in one facility to a quality-control cell pool run with tumors [@selitsky2020]. Over 65% of viral sequences from 712 libraries group with reagents or protocols rather than specimens [@asplund2019], and reanalyses have invalidated major archive-scale microbial findings [@gihawi2023]. Our safeguards are not individually new [@cantalupo2019]; our contribution is quantifying the size of each artifact rather than merely asserting it.

Petabase-scale surveys are now the standard way to establish viral presence across body sites, but a presence catalog cannot measure activity, and because they rely on assembly, integrated genomes fail to assemble across the virus-host junction; we show in @supptbl-e2 that the resulting E2 statistic cannot distinguish cervical carcinoma from skin and so cannot read genome state.

Several limitations apply. Archival sampling is non-random, so the absolute healthy-skin rate is an estimate. Sequencing chemistry could be resolved for only `r pp(stats$chem_pct)`% of libraries, and input amount, RNA integrity and fragment selection are unrecoverable from archived metadata. Because biopsy averaging dilutes focal transcription, our productivity estimates are a conservative lower bound. Finally, tissue and diagnosis labels are programmatic and imperfect, viral typing is constrained by the reference panel, and the data are cross-sectional, so these results describe phenomenology rather than prove a mechanism.

Cutaneous HPV is therefore productive in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis but leaves only a trace, non-productive footprint in cutaneous squamous neoplasia, regardless of sequencing depth or library chemistry. This phenotype is the baseline any theory of beta-HPV in skin cancer must address. Because all major hypotheses predict it, more precise measurement of viral activity will not separate them. That requires designs which break the shared prediction: matched DNA and RNA profiling across the precursor-to-carcinoma transition, spatial resolution of residual viral particles relative to mutant clones and infiltrating T cells, and interventional studies. Single-cell resolution has been demonstrated in cutaneous lesions [@devitt2019]; the next step is applying it at cohort scale across that transition.
